group.title: Small useful words
group.tagline: In, on, who, what and more
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Inside a thing or place.
wrong: The fish lives in the sky.

words.meaning: Touching the top of something.
wrong: The ceiling is on the floor.

words.meaning: Used to say the place or time of something.
wrong: I sleep at the moon every night.

words.meaning: Lower than something and below it.
wrong: The sky is under our feet.

words.meaning: Higher than something or above it.
wrong: The fish swam over the bottom of the sea, in the sand.

words.meaning: Showing where a person or thing started.
wrong: I walked from my house, and I started at school.

words.meaning: Together; having someone or something next to you.
wrong: I went with my friend, so I went alone.

words.meaning: Not having something.
wrong: I came without my bag, so here it is in my hand.

words.meaning: Used to show who will get something.
wrong: I bought a gift for you, so it is mine.

words.meaning: On the subject of.
wrong: The film is about cars, but there are no cars in it.

words.meaning: Moving to the inside of something.
wrong: He walked into the room and stayed outside.

words.meaning: Next to; also, using a way of travel.
wrong: I came by bus, so I walked all the way.

words.meaning: On every side of; in a circle.
wrong: We sat around the table, all on one side.

words.meaning: In the space within something.
wrong: The bird is inside the cage, flying in the open sky.

words.meaning: Not in a building or place.
wrong: The children played outside the house in their bedroom.

words.meaning: Higher than something.
wrong: The roof is above the floor and under the door.

words.meaning: A question word for asking which person.
wrong: Who is your teacher? It’s a red pencil.

words.meaning: A question word for asking about a thing.
wrong: What is your name? I’m ten.

words.meaning: A question word for picking one from a small group.
examples: {Which} color do you like, red or blue?
wrong: Which one do you want? Yes, thanks.

words.meaning: A question word for asking about a place.
wrong: Where is the bank? It’s at three o’clock.

words.meaning: A question word for asking about a time.
wrong: When is the party? It’s in the garden.

words.meaning: A question word for asking the reason.
wrong: Why are you late? I’m in the kitchen.

words.meaning: A question word for asking the way something is done.
wrong: How do you get to school? On Monday.

words.meaning: A word for a man or boy we already know about.
examples: This is Tom. {He} is my brother.
wrong: My mother is tall, and he is a doctor.

words.meaning: A word for a woman or girl we already know about.
examples: This is Anna. {She} is my sister.
wrong: My father is a cook, and she likes pasta.

words.meaning: A word for a thing or animal we already know about.
examples: I have a cat. {It} is black.
wrong: My aunt is a teacher, and it is very kind.

words.meaning: A word for me and other people.
wrong: I live all alone, and we are one person.

words.meaning: A word for two or more people or things.
examples: Tom and Ben are friends. {They} play football.
wrong: My only sister is ten, and they like music.

words.meaning: The person or people someone is talking to.
wrong: I’m talking to myself, so you are me.

words.meaning: A word the speaker uses for himself or herself.
wrong: Give me the ball, so I never get it.

words.meaning: A word for two or more people or things, after a verb.
examples: I love my cats. I feed {them} every day.
wrong: I have one dog and I walk them.

words.meaning: A word for joining two things together.
wrong: I have a cat and a dog, so I have only one pet.

words.meaning: A word to add a different idea.
examples: I like dogs, {but} I don’t like cats.
wrong: I’m hungry, but I want to eat.

words.meaning: A word to give a choice.
wrong: You can have tea or coffee, so you must drink both.

words.meaning: A word to give the reason.
examples: I’m tired {because} I worked all day.
wrong: I’m hungry because I just ate a big lunch.

words.meaning: A word to say what can happen when something else happens.
wrong: If it rains, we’ll get wet in the sun.

words.meaning: In this place, near me.
examples: Come {here} and sit next to me.
wrong: I’m here, far away in another country.

words.meaning: In that place, not near me.
wrong: The shop is there, right here in my hand.

words.meaning: A word that makes another word stronger.
wrong: It’s very hot today, just a little warm.

words.meaning: Too; as well.
examples: I speak English. I {also} speak French.
wrong: I like tea. I also don’t like anything.
